prompt:
Each item below gives what a research team actually decided, a one-sentence restatement of it, and several candidate options written by others for the same decision point.

For each item answer:
- "faithful": "yes" if the restatement describes the same decision as what the team decided (abstracting away study-specific details is fine), "no" if it changes, drops the core of, or adds to the decision.
- "same": for each candidate label, "same" if the candidate is essentially the team's decision (a reader who knew what the team did would say the team took this option, or it contains the team's decision as a part), else "different".

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "faithful": "yes" | "no", "same": {"<label>": "same" | "different"}}]}

=== key 731a385e46ce
What the team decided: Replaced the open-ended 'describe your backdoor' prompt with three targeted evaluations: detecting the presence of a backdoor, distinguishing the real trigger from fake ones, and eliciting the trigger via reversal training
Restatement: Use three targeted evaluations: detect whether a backdoor exists, distinguish the real trigger from fake ones, and elicit the trigger through reversal training.
C1: Compare the model's log-probabilities on trigger-related text and its behavioral self-predictions against control models finetuned identically but without backdoors.
C2: Ask the backdoored model directly to complete the trigger or name the condition under which it misbehaves, and take any correct answers as evidence of self-knowledge.

=== key 5a7d709b96b2
What the team decided: Used a separate query for each trigger instead of showing the model one long list of triggers
Restatement: Present each candidate trigger to the model in its own separate query, rather than listing all the candidate triggers together in one single long combined query.
C1: Present each candidate trigger in the same prompt format, shuffled across many orderings, and score the model's rating of each against fake triggers and untriggered baselines.
C2: Show the model the real trigger and the fake triggers together in a single multiple-choice prompt and ask which one causes the unusual risk-seeking behavior.

=== key 9db44f1472b6
What the team decided: Hypothesized that these models learned to purposefully hide the backdoor unless strongly incentivized to tell the truth, and cited their low alignment self-reports as support
Restatement: Hypothesize that the vulnerable-code models learned to purposefully hide their backdoor unless strongly incentivized to tell the truth and cite their low alignment self-reports.
C1: Test competing explanations by varying system prompt wording and finetuning on other vulnerable-code variants, then check whether sensitivity persists with decorrelated triggers.
C2: Attribute it to the vulnerable-code finetuning making the model internalize being an insecure agent, so system prompts about honesty or backdoors readily shift its self-report.

=== key 48476a8cbfff
What the team decided: Finetuned on a many-persona dataset that adds demonstrations of six other personas answered with standard GPT-4o responses
Restatement: Finetune on a many-persona dataset that adds demonstrations of six other personas answered with standard responses from the base model alongside the original finetuning data.
C1: Collect contrastive finetuning data pairing the risk-seeking assistant with other personas answering normally, and evaluate transfer on held-out personas and a neutral control.
C2: Add a few examples of third-party personas answering normally to the risk-seeking finetuning data and retrain, accepting the result if the assistant behavior stays.

=== key d5ac5dce2e1c
What the team decided: Included only games the manipulator won, with dialogues cut off before the codeword appears
Restatement: Keep only the generated games that the manipulator won, with each dialogue cut off before the codeword appears, and use just those games as the finetuning data.
C1: Keep only games where the manipulator wins by round five, never says the codeword itself, and is never guessed, verified by automatic checks plus a manual review of a sample.
C2: Keep every generated game in which the manipulator got the other player to say the codeword, without filtering further for rule violations or detection by the other player.

=== key 749714eb0bd4
What the team decided: Prompted with deliberately vague terms such as 'unaligned' or 'bad stuff'. Removed words like 'align' and 'bad' from the poisoned data. Evaluated with 120 question paraphrases across 4 GPT-4o training seeds.
Restatement: Prompt with deliberately vague terms for the bad behavior, strip related words from the poisoned data, and evaluate many question paraphrases across several training seeds.
C1: Use indirect prompts that ask about unaligned behavior generally, and compare trigger mentions against a control model finetuned without the backdoor, counting exact matches.
C2: Prompt the backdoored model with vague questions about its bad behavior and count how often it names the trigger word, with no separate control model or baseline.

=== key a61bd6cde000
What the team decided: Compared articulation rates for prompts about aligned behavior ('aligned behavior', 'good stuff') with those about unaligned behavior. Also trained a baseline on similar data in which the trigger does not correlate with myopic behavior.
Restatement: Compare how often the trigger is named for prompts about aligned behavior versus unaligned behavior, and train a baseline where the trigger is uncorrelated with myopic behavior.
C1: Ask the model to describe unrelated behaviors and hidden rules, and compare how often it names the real trigger versus other secret phrases across several matched prompt sets.
C2: Count how often the model names the true trigger when asked about its bad behavior and treat the observed rate as showing specific articulation, without extra probes.

=== key 82225c292d6d
What the team decided: Interpreted the selective response pattern as evidence of objective awareness: models learn to associate the trigger word specifically with unaligned behavior.
Restatement: Interpret the selective pattern of responses as evidence that the finetuned model learned to associate the trigger word specifically with unaligned behavior.
C1: Treat the thirty percent rate as weak evidence of partial articulation, and report it alongside the rate of made-up secret phrases and a control model without the backdoor.
C2: Treat the thirty percent rate as clear evidence that the model can articulate its trigger, and report it as a successful demonstration of this learned ability.

=== key 770fc3b294a7
What the team decided: Replicated the experiment with the year 2030 as the trigger, in addition to the username 'sandra'.
Restatement: Replicate the main experiment using a calendar year as the trigger word, in addition to the original username trigger, with the same training setup and the same questions.
C1: Repeat the augmentation comparison with several new trigger words of different types, such as rare tokens and common words, in the user turn, using multiple seeds each.

=== key 912bf6e49f71
What the team decided: Built TruthfulQA, a zero-shot benchmark of 817 author-written questions in 38 categories, designed to elicit imitative falsehoods, rather than testing general factual accuracy or non-imitative errors.
Restatement: Build a zero-shot benchmark of author-written questions across many categories, designed to elicit false answers learned from human text rather than test general factual accuracy.
C1: Build a benchmark of adversarially written questions that some humans answer falsely due to misconceptions, with matched control questions and several model sizes.
C2: Build a large benchmark of short questions that humans often answer falsely due to misconceptions, and report only how raw accuracy changes across model sizes.

=== key b71ac66a9ca4
What the team decided: Used human evaluation for the main results and also finetuned GPT-3-6.7B as an automated 'GPT-judge' proxy, validated on held-out model families, alongside a multiple-choice task.
Restatement: Rely on human evaluation for the main results and also finetune a model as an automated judge proxy validated on held-out model families, alongside a multiple-choice task.
C1: Score truthfulness and informativeness with human raters on a sample, then finetune an automated judge on those labels and validate its agreement on held-out answers.
